comparator.name: Information Science (Informatiekunde)
comparator.sourceNotes: The dated UvA study guide sets 60 required credits in year one, 48 required and 12 restricted-choice credits in year two, and 30 open, 24 required and 6 restricted-choice credits in year three. The illustrated choices retain Regulatory Compliant Information Systems and Semantic Web in year two and Logic and Society in year three. Reflection on Digital Culture and the final project are required.
components: Year two requires two of three courses: this course, Semantic Web and Recommender Systems. This example includes the first two named here.
Builds on programming, databases and introductory logic. Basic web development knowledge is recommended.
Builds on descriptive statistics and applies research methods to human-computer interaction.
UvA recommends advanced programming and prior Research Methods for Interactive Systems.
Choose 30 EC in the first semester of year three.
Required in year three alongside the final project and one of two restricted electives.
This example selects Logic and Society. Social Robotics is the other option.
Complete all 60 EC from each of the first two years before starting. The Board of Examiners can grant an individual exemption.

core: Information systems, programming, databases and computational modelling
Human-computer interaction, user-centred design and technology use
Organisations, socio-technical systems and societal effects of technology
Research methods, statistics, data analysis and system evaluation
adjacent: Responsible data use, privacy, ethics and digital governance
Data science, machine learning and decision support
Human cognition, interaction and experience with digital systems
questions: How can information systems connect data, organisational processes and user needs?
How can data and machine learning support analysis and decisions responsibly?
How do digital systems shape individual behaviour, organisations and society?

courses: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: Examines how organisations adopt AI and how regulation, work and governance shape its use.
Uses interviews, requirements and iterative prototypes to turn customer needs into product designs.
Uses customer journeys and primary and secondary evidence to evaluate experience and engagement.
Develops a strategy for digital change and examines how digital technology affects business models and responsibilities.
Plans and carries out customer research, analyses findings and turns evidence into recommendations.
Uses design thinking to test customer needs and build a startup plan across business functions.
Develops sampling, measurement and inference, and applies them in an empirical group project.
Studies organisational behaviour, culture, structure and change and develops a research plan and evidence review.
Examines AI fairness, privacy and responsibility through ethical theories and cases.
Uses sets, relations and formal proof to model and reason about computational problems.
Implements heuristic search, numerical optimisation and constraint satisfaction and evaluates their performance.
Investigates protocols, concurrency, scheduling and storage through network and systems exercises.
Uses relational modelling, SQL, normalisation and authorisation to structure and query information.
Analyses and tests data structures and algorithms for search, graphs and other computational tasks.
Implements and analyses advanced algorithms for matrix multiplication, Fourier transforms and optimisation.
Cleans, joins and visualises tabular, text and spatial datasets in R.
Builds prediction and classification models and compares them on held-out data.
Trains and evaluates neural networks for tabular data, images, text or time series.
Writes, tests and debugs structured and object-oriented Python programmes.
Uses calculus and differential equations to build and interpret a dynamic model.
Uses vectors, matrices, transformations and decompositions in modelling and data analysis.
Implements numerical methods for equations, integration and dynamical models, checking error and stability.
Uses differential equations and Fourier methods to model signals and feedback.
Uses probability, estimation, Bayesian reasoning and simulation to quantify uncertainty.
Applies ethical theories and critical argument to practical problems and responsibility.
Uses sociological theories to interpret networks, institutions, identity and inequality.
Develops interviews, observation, coding and thematic analysis for studying people and organisations.
Investigates trust, social capital and participation in civil-society groups and networks.
Studies sensory processing and goal-directed action using cognitive-neuroscience evidence.
Studies attention, memory and cognitive control and tests attention in an experiment.
Introduces behavioural and neural explanations of learning, cognition and social influence.
Studies group behaviour, social influence and persuasion and develops an empirical research proposal.
Fits and interprets statistical models for behavioural research and evaluates experimental design.
Uses systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the strength and consistency of behavioural evidence.
Tests persuasive framing and communication choices in applied projects on behaviour change.

alternatives.label: Information systems, data and digital society
alternatives.concept: Study how organisations collect, store and use information. Combine programming, databases and data analysis with qualitative research, product design and the study of technology-driven change.
alternatives.labelReason: Computing, user research, product design and organisational change share the focus.
progression: Programming precedes networks and algorithms. Research and data foundations precede machine learning, market research and advanced modelling.

alternatives.label: Data science and computational information
alternatives.concept: Use mathematics and computing to analyse information. Study probability, numerical methods and signals, then build and assess models using advanced algorithms and machine learning.
alternatives.labelReason: Linear algebra, numerical methods, signals, probability and advanced algorithms form a distinct mathematical sequence.
alternatives.distinctness: 5 courses (37.5 EC) differ from the broad option in each direction. The differences concentrate on mathematical and algorithmic methods.
progression: Mathematical Methods precedes linear algebra, numerical methods, linear systems and probability. Algorithms & Data Structures precedes Advanced Algorithms.

alternatives.label: Human-centred and socio-technical systems
alternatives.concept: Investigate how people perceive, use and respond to technology. Combine computing foundations with cognition, qualitative research, customer journeys and product design.
alternatives.labelReason: Cognition, social and organisational behaviour, research synthesis and user-centred projects form a sustained strand.
alternatives.distinctness: 7 courses differ from the broad option and 11 from the data-science option in each direction. The differences concentrate on cognition, behaviour, design and evidence about users.
progression: Brain & Behavior precedes the cognition courses and advanced evidence synthesis. Research foundations precede customer-engagement and market-research projects.

selection.assessment: The broad programme addresses computing, users and organisational information. The data option deepens mathematics and algorithms. The human-centred option develops cognition, qualitative inquiry and the study of users. Each pair clears the distinctness floor, and the three-option limit applies.

blocks: Data, information systems and computational modelling
Both use structured programming, collections, functions and introductory classes.
Both explore unfamiliar datasets and communicate patterns with graphics. UCR combines visualisation with data preparation in R.
Both design and query relational databases. UvA also compares other database paradigms.
Both teach formal logic, sets, relations and reasoning with proofs.
Both compare and evaluate machine-learning methods on datasets and address issues such as overfitting.
Both build and evaluate deep-learning models in Python across data types. UvA combines this with a broader data science pipeline.
Both use vectors and matrices for applied problems. UvA’s introductory course also includes calculus and probability.
Both examine how technology and strategy shape organisations. UvA focuses on the management and sharing of information and knowledge.
Both use research on user needs, design requirements and iterative prototypes. UvA concentrates on interactive digital systems.
Both study perception and the processes that guide responses. UvA also includes memory and a behavioural research project.
Both develop academic communication, reflection and responsible academic practice. UvA teaches these in a short practicum within a multi-course sequence.
Both use behavioural study design and statistics. UvA applies them to a team project about interaction with technology.
Both apply ethical theories to digital technology, privacy and social responsibility. UCR concentrates on AI.

notes.text: UCR combines computing, data analysis, user research and the study of organisations across several disciplines. UvA also teaches Semantic Web, information-system compliance and a sequence of dedicated system projects. Its individual final project is compulsory.

audience.programmeDescription: Information Science at the University of Amsterdam studies how people and organisations design and use digital systems. Students learn programming, data analysis and interaction design and apply these skills in team projects and an individual final project.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR options emphasise information and organisations, mathematical data analysis, or how people use technology. UvA combines these themes in one programme with a dedicated sequence of information-system design and research projects.
